scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Regency dance covers the period from roughly 1790 to 1825, extending beyond the historical 1811–1820 regency of George IV.
In the early decades, longways country dances, French cotillions, and scotch reels dominated English ballrooms.
The 1810s saw major shifts: the waltz arrived in England around 1810, causing moral debate over close partner contact, while Lady Jersey introduced the French quadrille in 1815.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dance served as a major social ritual for courtship, status display, and community assembly during the late Georgian and Regency eras.
Leading a longways set held high social honor, granting the top lady authority over the figures and music for the dance.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances of this era were bouncy and lively rather than smooth or solemn.
Longways country dances featured two lines of partners performing figures, with the top lady choosing figures and steps before dancing down to the bottom of the set.
Cotillions were danced in a square, alternating standard changes (such as a right-hand star or moulinet) with unique chorus figures.
Watch for Setting, Heying, Moulinet.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for Regency dances varied according to the specific format, including country dance tunes, reels, and imported French or German pieces.
Meter ranged from 3/4 time for the standard waltz to 2/4 time for the sauteuse and various meters for quadrille and country dance figures.
The pulse is 2/4 or 3/4 depending on the specific dance.
Bright, structured dance music supporting energetic skipping, setting, and stepping across various meters.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Jane Austen famously depicted assembly balls in her novels and described calling dances in her letters.
Lady Jersey introduced the quadrille to London high society in 1815.
Regional forms included the French cotillion and quadrille, the Scottish scotch reel, and late-period country dance adaptations like the Danse Espagnuole (Spanish dance) and Danse Ecossoise.

Regency country dance descended from traditional English Country Dance and contributed to later nineteenth-century social dances, including the American Virginia Reel (derived from Sir Roger de Coverley).

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Regency dance is parent of English Country Dance: Regency country dance represents a specific historical era of the broader English Country Dance tradition.
Regency dance is child of Quadrille: The quadrille was introduced to England in 1815 and gradually eclipsed older longways country dances.
Regency dance is variant of Waltz: The early Regency waltz was danced on the balls of the feet with a slower tempo and distinct arm positions.
Regency dance is child of Virginia Reel: Derived from the Regency-era dance Sir Roger de Coverley.
